questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion drawn from the absence of a refutation
questions.learningObjective: identify an inference from the absence of evidence to a claim of falsehood
questions.stem: A member argues that nobody has ever produced a case in which the seminar's new logging system lost a record, and concludes from that silence that the system cannot lose records. What is the argument doing?

options.text: Reading the absence of a refutation as a refutation, so silence is being treated as a verdict on the claim
Reading the absence of a refutation as a confirmation, so silence is being treated as a verdict for the claim
options.misconception: credits the argument with the opposite conclusion, since the member denies rather than asserts the claim

options.text: Demanding a standard of proof the system was never asked to meet, since a burden of that kind applies to new claims only
options.misconception: moves the objection from the inference to the standard of proof, which is not where this argument fails

options.text: Describing a claim about frequency as though it were a claim about possibility, so a different question is being answered
options.misconception: recasts the fault as a confusion between two kinds of question, which is not the inference at issue

questions.explanation: This is the argument from ignorance, and its shape is always the same: a claim is treated as defeated by the failure of anyone to produce a case against it. A claim normally stands until something counts against it, so the burden lies on the member who says the system does lose records, and silence on that side leaves the claim untouched rather than settled. The direction matters, which is why the second option is wrong: reading silence as confirmation would be the mirror error, and the member is denying the claim, not asserting it. The third option raises a fair question in the abstract but does not describe what was said, and the fourth mistakes a claim about how often something occurs for a claim about whether it can occur at all.
questions.hint: Ask where the burden of proof has been placed, and whether the silence is being read as evidence for or against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Answering a criticism with the critic's own practice
questions.learningObjective: recognise a reply that turns a criticism back on the person making it
questions.stem: Asked why the group's shared reading notes are incomplete, a member replies that the colleague raising this has not finished half the assigned texts. How should the room classify that reply?

options.text: A concession, since both members now accept the fault exists and only dispute who ought to put it right
options.misconception: reads the reply as agreement about the fault, when the member has accepted nothing and denied the charge

options.text: A request for evidence, since the reply is asking the criticism to be substantiated before the group acts on it
options.misconception: mistakes a deflection for an evidential demand, since no evidence is asked for anywhere in the reply

options.text: A distinction, since it separates the group's shared notes from the individual habits being complained about
options.misconception: recasts a personal attack as a conceptual separation, which is the opposite of what the reply does

options.text: A tu quoque, since the practicer of a fault cannot show that the criticism of the fault is mistaken

questions.explanation: The reply commits the tu quoque: it answers a question about the state of the group's notes by pointing at the standing of the person who asked. Whether the colleague has finished the assigned texts is a separate matter, and no answer to it changes the fact that the notes are incomplete. The reply survives in the room only because it shifts attention, and a reader can dispose of it in one move by setting the two questions side by side and answering each on its own. None of the other classifications fits: nothing is conceded, no evidence is requested, and no line is drawn between the collective record and one member's habits, since the reply deliberately keeps them together.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything the colleague said or did could make the group's shared notes complete.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Defending a practice by how long it has been in use
questions.learningObjective: identify a practice defended by its duration rather than its merit
questions.stem: A department has assessed first drafts on the same five-point scale for nine years. When a member proposes replacing it, a colleague answers that the scale is the way it is because previous members chose it. How does the reply treat the history?

options.text: As evidence about standing, since the members who chose the scale outrank the member proposing change
options.misconception: supplies a claim about rank that the reply does not make, turning a practice into a matter of seniority

options.text: As an opening for the meeting, since an inherited arrangement gives a group its first shared object to examine
options.misconception: reads the remark as conversation-opening rather than as a defence that closes the question off

options.text: As a warrant for the practice, so nine years of use is offered in place of a reason the scale marks well
As a reason for caution, so changing an arrangement that has worked needs more argument than one untried
options.misconception: reframes a bare appeal to tradition as prudence, which grants the reply a standard it never invoked

questions.explanation: The reply offers duration in place of merit. How long an arrangement has survived is a fact about its history, and it bears on a practice only through some stated connection between longevity and accuracy, which is a claim a person can be wrong about and the reply does not make. Nine years of use would support the scale if the reason added were that markers became well calibrated on it, and the group could then argue about that reason. Without the step, the history is doing the work that a reason should do, and it is work a number of years cannot do. The other options each add something the reply does not contain: a standard of caution, a claim about rank, or a conversational purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what the nine years would have to show about the scale for the reply to be a reason rather than a fact.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Defending a method by when it appeared
questions.learningObjective: state what an argument from recency would need in order to support a recommendation
questions.stem: A member backs a new peer-review protocol on one ground: it was written after group chats became a project's normal way to talk to a supervisor, unlike the printed memo it replaces. What has to be supplied for that ground to support the recommendation?

options.text: A quotation from a supervisor calling the memo unusable, since grounds of that kind are seldom disputed
options.misconception: proposes a testimonial where a connection is missing, which strengthens the case without filling the gap

options.text: A reason the change in how a project talks should make the review of its work better, not merely newer
A count of how many projects now hold supervisor conversations by chat, since frequency shows the practice is normal
options.misconception: supplies a measure of how common the practice is, which does not connect to the quality of a review

options.text: A statement of the reviewer time the protocol saves, since an old format is a cost the group has absorbed
options.misconception: adds an efficiency criterion the member never invoked, so it supports the protocol on other grounds

questions.explanation: The argument offers a coincidence of dates as though it were a connection. What has changed is the mode of conversation between a project and its supervisor; the protocol is a procedure for reviewing work. An argument from recency is completed only by a step that joins those two, saying why conversations in the new mode create work that the new procedure handles better. Add that step and the member has a case, which the group can then dispute. The other three would each make the recommendation better supported while leaving the actual gap open: one establishes how ordinary chats are, one establishes a saving in time, one supplies a voice against the old format, and none of them says why the change in conversation makes a review better.
questions.hint: Ask what connects the way a project talks to its supervisor with the way its work is reviewed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A chain of consequences asserted without steps
questions.learningObjective: locate the unsupported steps in a slippery-slope argument
questions.stem: A member opposes letting the group record discussions on phones by arguing that once recording is permitted, anything said in a seminar can be held against the speaker later, and eventually the group will say nothing at all. Which part of the argument carries the load?

options.text: The member's preference for a silent group, which is a value the room is entitled to weigh on its own terms
options.misconception: reduces the argument to a preference, leaving the two unsupported consequence steps unexamined

options.text: The two unexamined steps from permitting recording to total silence, neither of which is supported at all
The step from a present rule to what later users do with a recording, which is the part the member cannot control
options.misconception: picks out a real difficulty and treats it as the fault, when the reply raises it as support for the rule

options.text: The step asserting that phones can make a usable recording, which is the technical question the rule turns on
options.misconception: supposes the argument doubts the recording is possible, whereas it accepts the step and goes further

questions.explanation: A slippery slope is not wrong because it predicts a bad outcome; it is wrong because the steps between the decision and the outcome are asserted rather than argued. Here the first step, that a recording may later be used against a speaker, is plausible and the member may well be right to weigh it. The second step, that this will happen often enough to silence the group, is a different claim and needs its own support, which is not offered anywhere in the argument. A member who wanted to keep the objection alive would have to say what makes the second step likely, and could reasonably expect the room to contest it. What the argument as given does is present its conclusion as the inevitable terminus of a sequence nobody has examined.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate claims the chain contains, and how many of them have been argued.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The bad outcome offered as proof of a motive
questions.learningObjective: identify a claim about what someone intended that is supported by what an intention would cost
questions.stem: A member argues that the outside archive's new access fee must have been set to raise revenue, on the ground that a fee designed to widen access would have cost the archive money and no institution gives money away. How is the claim about motive being supported?

options.text: By the size of the fee, which would show the archive chose revenue once the amount charged were known
options.misconception: names an evidential route the reply does not take, since no figure for the fee appears anywhere in it

options.text: By the archive's other charges, since a settled pattern of prices would indicate which aim had been chosen
options.misconception: proposes a pattern of evidence absent from the argument, which reasons from one instance only

options.text: By the absence of a stated purpose, since an undeclared aim is the one a body is taken to be acting on
options.misconception: turns a claim about cost into a claim about silence, which the argument never appeals to

options.text: By what the two intentions would cost, so the case runs from consequences to what the setters intended

questions.explanation: The member wants a conclusion about intention, which is a claim about what people in the archive were trying to do, and supplies a premise about money instead. The inference from cost to intention is an appeal to consequences: it establishes, at most, that a revenue aim would have been costly under the opposite intention, and says nothing about which aim was adopted. This is worth separating from a case where consequences are the right consideration. If the member's claim had been that the group should not pay the fee because of what payment leads to, the reasoning would be sound. The claim is about what the setters meant, and money cannot establish that. The room can ask what would: an internal document, a stated aim, or a pattern in the archive's other charges.
questions.hint: Ask whether the conclusion is about what happened next or about what the setters intended.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Discrediting a claim by who produced it
questions.learningObjective: identify the fallacy of origin and state what the room should have asked instead
questions.stem: A member reports that the city's parking-charge revenue rose by nine per cent over a year, and hears another member call the figure unreliable because it came from a body funded by parking operators. What has the second member done?

options.text: Treated an interest in the figure as settling its accuracy, so the source is disqualified without a claim about the figure
Treated interested sources as unusable in principle, so the group could not use this or any published figure
options.misconception: turns a remark about one figure into a rule about sources, which the speaker did not propose

options.text: Treated the figure as describing a period too old to bear on the present, since older counts are harder to check
options.misconception: invokes an objection about the figure's age, which appears nowhere in the remark that was made

options.text: Treated the absence of a second count as proof the figure is wrong, since one source is treated as none at all
options.misconception: moves from a claim about the source to a claim about the figure being false, which is not what was said

questions.explanation: This is the fallacy of origin, and it is seductive because an interest in a result really is a reason to look harder. What it is not is a reason to have already decided. From a funded body we may properly ask how the figure was gathered, whether the accounting basis was the same as in the previous year, and whether the body had anything to gain by the choice. Those questions might still leave the figure unusable. The remark made none of them: it moved straight from who published the number to the number's being unreliable, and in doing so treated a fact about the source as if it were a fact about the figure. An interest is a reason for scrutiny, and the room has just been given the most common reason for being wrong about a number.
questions.hint: Ask what a funded source gives you a reason to check, and what it gives you a reason to conclude.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Discrediting an argument before it is made
questions.learningObjective: recognise a remark that attacks an argument in advance rather than answering it
questions.stem: Before a member can put her case, another member says that anyone who reaches her conclusion does so because they were not in the room last term and missed the discussion that settles the matter. How should the room treat the remark?

options.text: As a fair warning about the discussion, which a member may properly make before hearing a case out
options.misconception: grants the remark the standing it was designed to avoid, so the case is never put to the room

options.text: As a request for evidence, since the speaker is being asked to establish that she attended last term
options.misconception: mistakes a dismissal for an evidential demand, since attendance is not what the remark turns on

options.text: As an attack on the case's expected speaker, which discourages hearing the argument rather than meeting it
As a claim about who was present, which the attendance record settles either way on the facts
options.misconception: reads the remark as a factual dispute to be settled, when it is offered to dispose of a case unheard

questions.explanation: The remark does not touch the case because the case has not been heard. It addresses the person likely to make it and predicts the reason she will reach her conclusion, and a room that accepts the prediction has a reason not to listen, which is the whole point of the move. The honest reply is to notice that the prediction was made in advance, and to ask what a member who had been in the room last term but reached the same conclusion would be told. If the answer is that they too would be suspected, the remark was never about attendance at all. The other three readings each grant the remark a job it was not doing: checking a fact, flagging a caution, or requesting evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the room would be doing if it accepted the prediction, and whether the case has been heard.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A possibility treated as a probability
questions.learningObjective: identify a step from what could happen to what should be expected
questions.stem: A member objects to a plan for a shared archive on the ground that a contributor could one day withdraw consent and remove material other members have already built on. What has the objection established?

options.text: That the material should be copied before use, since duplication would protect the group from a withdrawal
options.misconception: supplies a remedy the objection never mentions, and in fact cannot defeat a withdrawal of consent

options.text: That withdrawal is possible, and moved to the plan being unsafe without saying how likely withdrawal is
That the plan is unsafe, and left the possibility of harm as a second and separate reason to refuse it
options.misconception: reports the objection as complete, when the likelihood step is precisely the part left unargued

options.text: That consent was the wrong basis for the archive, since a withdrawal right was always going to be exercised
options.misconception: adds a claim about the basis of the plan, which the objection about withdrawal does not reach

questions.explanation: The member moves from a possibility to an expectation without marking the move. Withdrawal is indeed available to any contributor, and the room may reasonably decide that a right it cannot renounce is a real constraint; that is a judgement about how much the plan depends on others continuing. What has not been shown is that the right will be exercised, or often enough to matter. The two claims are separable, and the objection as given argues the first and needs the second. A reply can supply the second in either direction, and the group can compare plans by how much weight each gives to it, which is impossible while the step between the two is unmarked. Copying material, incidentally, is not a way out: a withdrawal of consent reaches the copy too.
questions.hint: Ask how often the thing being objected to would have to happen before the plan's safety was in question.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A term doing different work in each premise
questions.learningObjective: detect the shifting middle term in an argument with two true premises
questions.stem: A member argues that the marking policy proves the department is understaffed: every tutor on the policy is on the review panel, and every member of the review panel is on the department's staff. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The middle term means the tutors in the first premise and the staff in the second, so nothing joins the two
Two true premises cannot produce a false conclusion, so the staffing claim must follow from the membership claim
options.misconception: denies the possibility of a valid form with a false conclusion, which is exactly the case on display

options.text: The conclusion restates a premise, so the argument adds nothing and should be dropped from the discussion
options.misconception: treats a faulty argument as a redundant one, which is a different complaint about the same speech

options.text: The premises describe the panel and the conclusion describes staffing, so a further premise is required
options.misconception: names a real missing premise while ignoring the shift that makes the two membership claims unrelated

questions.explanation: The argument has the shape of a syllogism and it is the middle term that fails. The first premise says that anyone who writes on the marking policy sits on the review panel, so the word the argument needs is tutor. The second says that anyone on the review panel sits on the department's staff, so the word it supplies is staff. The argument therefore runs from tutors to tutors and never reaches staffing, and the conclusion is about a group neither premise was stated to cover. This is why the two premises can both be true and the conclusion false, which is a fact about form rather than about anyone's honesty. The fourth option is a real observation, and adding a premise about how many staff are needed for a review panel would give the group something worth arguing about.
questions.hint: Write out the two membership claims as sets, and see whether the second takes up the first's membership.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Judging a procedure by an outcome it produced
questions.learningObjective: identify the appeal to the result in two opposed forms
questions.stem: A pilot produces one successful placement out of four. One member argues the pilot's design was sound because it worked, and another argues it was unsound because the other three failed. What do the two members share?

options.text: Both rely on a base far too small, so the disagreement is about numbers rather than about the design
options.misconception: moves the dispute onto sample size, which neither member mentioned and which does not settle a design

options.text: Both assume a success and a failure count equally, which is why the room cannot choose between them
options.misconception: invents a shared assumption about evidential weight, which the two speakers never advanced

options.text: Both have mistaken the pilot for a trial, which is a fault in how the two describe what was run
options.misconception: supplies a shared confusion about terminology that the argument, as given, does not rest on

options.text: Both read the outcome as a verdict on the design, when an outcome shows a result and not what produced it

questions.explanation: Both members commit the appeal to the result, one in each direction, and noticing that symmetry is what makes the item teach. An outcome is produced by a design together with everything else that happened: who the four were, what else was in the labour market that term, whether anyone followed up with them. A design is judged by whether the procedure, run as described, would be expected to produce the result, and that question cannot be answered by pointing at the result itself. This is not a small sample point, which is a separate criticism and a good one, since four placements tell us little whatever the design was. The reviewer of this argument should ask what the design would have predicted, and whether what happened matches, because the two members are arguing past the only question that would settle the disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask what the design would have predicted, and then whether what happened matches that prediction.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Past expenditure offered as a reason to continue
questions.learningObjective: identify the sunk cost error in a decision about ongoing work
questions.stem: A committee has spent two years and most of its budget on a shared catalogue. Asked whether the catalogue is worth continuing, a member answers that stopping now would waste everything already put in. What is that answer?

options.text: A defence of the committee's earlier judgement, since spending two years shows the plan was chosen well
options.misconception: turns a reply about the future into a vindication of the past, which is a different defence

options.text: A reminder that members gave their time, which the committee is accountable for alongside the budget
options.misconception: invokes a cost the member never named, and time already given is as spent as the money

options.text: An argument from what is already spent, when the question is what further spending would buy
A statement that the catalogue is finished, which settles the question of continuing without more discussion
options.misconception: reports a claim about completion, which the member neither makes nor needs in order to answer

questions.explanation: The money is gone either way. Whatever the committee decides today, the two years and the budget are spent, so the difference between continuing and stopping is the difference between what the next year costs and what the next year brings. To argue for continuing, a member has to compare the catalogue's future value against what else the money could buy, and the reply does not do this; it counts something that is unaffected by the choice. The error is easy to commit precisely because a large past investment feels like a stake, and feeling a stake is a fact about the committee rather than about the catalogue. A member who wanted to make the sunk-cost case honestly would have to argue that the earlier spending is a reason the project is further along than an equivalent project started now, which can be true and is a different argument.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money already spent would be recoverable by stopping, and how that affects the comparison.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An act excused by the same act done to the group
questions.learningObjective: identify a retributive justification and state what it does not settle
questions.stem: A member whose proposal was voted down withdraws a handout she had already promised to share, and justifies it by saying the group voted against her and is owed the same treatment. How should the room read that justification?

options.text: As a request for an apology, since withdrawing the handout is the pressure most likely to produce one
options.misconception: supplies a motive the member never stated, and motives do not settle a question of obligation

options.text: As a description of group practice, since withdrawing a handout is how this group routinely handles votes
options.misconception: promotes one member's response into a group convention, which no evidence in the case supplies

options.text: As a claim that a wrong suffered licenses the wrong in hand, which compares acts and settles nothing
As a reply about the vote itself, since the question in dispute is whether the vote was properly taken
options.misconception: redirects to the vote, which the member treats as settled and is not using as a complaint at all

questions.explanation: The justification reasons by analogy between two wrongs, and the analogy is the whole of it. That the group is owed a similar treatment is a claim about what the group has done, and it may well be true; it says nothing about whether the handout should be withheld. Two obligations can conflict here, since a promise was made and a decision was also reached, and the honest position is to name both rather than to trade on the injury. What the retributive form does is make the counter-consideration feel like a payment, which lets a member discharge a promise without addressing whether there is any reason to break it. If the handout is genuinely the group's property once promised, the group has an argument available; that argument would not rest on the vote having been unfair.
questions.hint: Ask what follows from the group having made a promise, and what follows from the group having voted.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A compromise offered as though it were balanced
questions.learningObjective: identify the assumption that makes a numerical compromise meaningless
questions.stem: A member says a reasonable settlement of the marking dispute is to keep three of the five criteria and drop two, on the grounds that a criterion kept is the same as a criterion half kept. What is the reply assuming?

options.text: That one settlement has been presented as the only one, which is how a compromise is used to end debate
options.misconception: describes a negotiating tactic, which may be present but is not the assumption being examined

options.text: That the two criteria dropped are less important, since that is what a reasonable group would keep and drop
options.misconception: adds a weighting the member never states, and a weighting would make the split less reasonable, not more

options.text: That the criteria are interchangeable units, when in fact they differ in how much a mark depends on each
That a numerical split is not yet an agreement, since a settlement still has to be argued for
options.misconception: raises a fair procedural point that has nothing to do with the reasoning error in the reply

questions.explanation: A count is only a count when the things counted are commensurable. Three of five criteria is a majority of the list and nothing at all about the marking, unless the criteria carry equal weight, and the reply's own supporting remark asserts that a kept criterion is a half-kept one, which is a claim about weights that nobody in this argument has established. Two teams of readers can weigh the same five criteria differently and reach opposite verdicts about which three to keep, and the arithmetic settles nothing between them. A workable version of the proposal would state how much the marking depends on each criterion and then drop from the bottom, which is a different argument and a better one. Note the second option: if the weights were known, the split might be indefensible, which is the point.
questions.hint: Ask what a criterion is worth in the marking, and whether the reply knows.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes one account of a pattern preferable to another
questions.learningObjective: weigh rival accounts by what each makes possible as against what each absorbs

stimulus.kind: position-paper written for this question
stimulus.body: Position paper prepared for this exercise. Seminar attendance fell in the term after a room change, from 61 of 90 members to 40 of 92. Three accounts are offered. The first is the room: the new room is a ten-minute walk from the old one and the building has no step-free route to it. The second is the schedule: the session moved from the afternoon to first thing in the morning. The third is that the group has told people for years that the sessions are optional and this term repeated the point in public. The paper records that the room changed in week three and the timetable changed in week seven, that attendance had already fallen in the two terms before either change, and that no membership records exist for who had a class before the morning start.

questions.stem: Taking only what the paper reports, which consideration gives the strongest reason to prefer the room account over the other two?

options.text: It is the only account with a stated mechanism, and a stated mechanism is more likely to be right
options.misconception: treats having a mechanism as a merit in itself, so an account that can absorb anything outranks a checkable one

options.text: It appears first among the three accounts, and a document's first account is usually the preferred one
options.misconception: uses the order of a document as evidence about the world, which is a fact about the writing and not the case

options.text: It is the only account that survives being dated, since the other two describe a term the paper omits
options.misconception: claims a coverage the paper does not have, since the paper dates the room and the timetable both

options.text: It is tied to a dated event whose timing the attendance record can be checked against, while the others fit any timing

questions.explanation: A good account of a pattern is one that risks something, in the sense that it says what should have been observed and could have come out otherwise. The room account makes a dated claim: if the walk and the step-free route are why people stayed away, the fall should begin in week three, when the room changed, and should be steeper for members who do not drive. The schedule account puts the fall in week seven, the optionality account predicts no particular week at all, and neither can be wrong about the pattern no matter what the record shows. That asymmetry is the strongest reason available from the paper, and it is a reason to prefer rather than to conclude: the same check can be run on attendance broken down by week and by how members travel, and it may yet weaken the room account. The other options substitute the presence of a mechanism, the order of the prose, and a coverage the paper does not claim for a reason the record can supply.
questions.hint: Ask what each account says should have been observed, and whether the record could have come out otherwise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The account that covers more of the period at issue
questions.learningObjective: compare two accounts of one fall by the period each can account for

stimulus.kind: memorandum written for this question
stimulus.body: Internal memorandum written for this exercise. Reading-group membership fell from 31 to 14 during a single term. Two accounts have been proposed to the group. The first is the meeting time: the session moved to a later slot three weeks into the term, and two members have said the new time does not work for them. The second is the notice: the group stopped sending a message about each meeting at the start of that term, and members began asking, in the thread afterwards, when the group met. The group's own record shows the message was not sent in any of the three weeks before the time change, and shows two new members joining in week two and leaving in week five without a stated reason.

questions.stem: What does the comparison of the two accounts, on the evidence the memorandum reports, show?

options.text: The notice account is preferred, because it is offered for the whole term and the time change cannot reach the first three weeks
The time account is preferred, because a stated obstacle is more credible than a lapsed routine nobody intended
options.misconception: prefers an account on how plausible the motive sounds, which is not what the coverage comparison shows

options.text: Neither is preferred, because both were formed after the fall and so cannot be weighed on how much they cover
options.misconception: dismisses the comparison because both accounts are post hoc, which bears on formation and not on coverage

options.text: Both are kept, since a term-long cause and a late-term cause may both contribute and nothing separates them
options.misconception: declines to weigh evidence the memorandum supplies, namely the notice lapsing before the change

questions.explanation: The membership fall of 17 covers the whole term, and one account is offered for the whole term while the other begins in week four. questions.hint: Ask when each change happened, and whether the fall it is supposed to explain was already under way.

questions.topic: A factor named only after the result was known
questions.learningObjective: identify a post hoc rescue and the reason it cannot explain the result

stimulus.kind: report extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Extract from a report written for this exercise. 'Group 4 recorded 11 failures in the first month after the change and 12 in the second, so the change did not improve the rate. We had expected the morning slot to help, because the two members who start early had told the officer who ran the change that mornings suited them. No one had proposed the morning slot as a reason for the failures before the change was made, and the officer passed the remark on in a single message without a note of when it was made.'

options.text: The officer had an interest in the outcome, so no report of a change should ever have been accepted
options.misconception: generalises into a rule about interested reporters, which would empty the file of most evidence

options.text: The remark concerned the slot rather than the failures, so it does not address the rate the extract records
options.misconception: confuses the subject of the remark with its bearing, since a slot that repels members is about failures

options.text: The reason was reached for after the result and reached through the officer who ran the change, so it cannot stand as an account of it
The two members were asked before the change rather than after, so their view cannot bear on why it failed
options.misconception: reverses the timing the extract reports, since the remark was made before the change was made

First, the factor was not in anyone's mind as a possible cause before the result was known, so it has been fitted to the outcome rather than having predicted it, which is what an explanation has to do. Second, it reached the file through the person who ran the change: a remark passed on in a single message, with no date, from an officer with a stake in the outcome, is not independent of the thing it is being used to explain. The report is honest about both, and stating them is the mark of careful work. The difficulty is not that the two members were wrong, since mornings may indeed suit them, but that this account of the failures was constructed after the fact by a party to the result, and a group that leaned on it would be leaning on the change's own account of its failure.
questions.hint: Ask whether the factor was in anyone's mind before the result, and how it reached the file.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Making two accounts of one event comparable
questions.learningObjective: state what rival accounts must differ in before evidence can tell them apart
questions.stem: A seminar's reading group fell from 31 to 14 in one term. Two accounts are on the table: the meeting time changed three weeks into the term, or the notice of each meeting stopped going out at the start of it. First say what rival accounts have to be like before the group can weigh them, then say what would tell them apart. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: The two must be given equal support, since an unfairly matched pair of accounts is a rigged comparison
options.misconception: asks for symmetry of support, which is not a property that two explanations can be required to share

options.text: The two must imply different records, since accounts that predict the same thing cannot be told apart by evidence
The two must cover the same period, since a cause outside the term cannot explain a fall inside it
options.misconception: supplies a necessary condition the group already meets, and mistakes it for the one that does the work

options.text: The two must be phrased in the same terms, since a difference of vocabulary would otherwise decide the weighing
options.misconception: makes a presentational requirement do the work of a evidential one, which is about records and not wording

questions.explanation: Two accounts can only be settled against each other if they disagree about what the world would look like. The time account says the meeting moved in week four, so the weeks before that should show the group intact; the notice account says members stopped hearing about meetings from week one, so the departures should be spread across the term rather than bunched after week four. Those are different records, and the group's own membership list can distinguish them, which is what the second stage is for. The other options are worth naming because each looks like a fairness condition and none is. Matching periods and phrasings make a comparison tidy rather than decisive, and demanding equal support confuses symmetry with rigor: an account supported by the record and an account resting on a lapsed routine are not an unfair pair, they are a pair in which one is better evidenced.
questions.hint: Ask what each account says should be visible in the record, and whether those two things differ.

questions.topic: An elimination resting on how the data were gathered
questions.learningObjective: identify the method feature that a conclusion about cause silently relies on

stimulus.kind: methods extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Methods extract written for this exercise. 'Of the 240 support tickets the group received this year, 61 were closed within two working days. Tickets mentioning the form were closed faster than tickets not mentioning it: 34 of 58 against 27 of 182. We therefore record the form as a cause of faster closure. Two of the four teams had used an earlier version of the form: 31 of 41 of their fast closures were form-related, against 3 of 17 for the team that used a redesigned form asking for the same details on a second page. No record was kept of how callers ranked their own tickets, so we have no comparison on that variable. A ticket counts as form-related if the caller's message mentions the form anywhere, and no ticket was counted twice.'

questions.stem: A reader concludes that the redesigned form is what made closure faster. Which feature of the extract most resists that conclusion?

options.text: No priority data was kept, so a difference in how the teams' callers ranked tickets could move with the form
The definition of form-related allowed a ticket in on any mention, so the two groups differ in size
options.misconception: describes a rule the extract applies equally, so it cannot by itself account for a difference between teams

options.text: No ticket was counted twice, so the totals for the two teams cannot be compared with each other
options.misconception: treats a rule preventing double counting as a bar to comparison, when it is the condition for it

options.text: Only 240 tickets were available, so the counts are too small to support any claim at all
options.misconception: answers a question about the total when the reader's claim concerns the split between two teams

questions.explanation: The reader's claim is a claim about cause, and the extract contains one variable that was never measured and would plausibly move with the form. A redesigned form that adds a second page is not the kind of change a team puts in place by accident, and teams that adopted it may also have been the teams handling urgent calls more attentively; if callers sorted their own tickets differently, the difference in fast closures would follow from the sorting rather than from the form. Everything else in the extract is a rule applied alike or a feature of the counting that makes the two teams comparable. The honest repair is not to drop the finding but to state what it is: form-related tickets closed faster, 34 of 58 against 27 of 182, which is 58.6 per cent against 14.8 per cent, a difference of about 44 percentage points that is descriptive until something is measured that could account for it.
questions.hint: Look for what the teams were not measured on, and ask whether it could have moved with the change.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A pattern the analyst was already looking for
questions.learningObjective: assess how much a confirmed prediction is worth when it was sought after the fact

stimulus.kind: report extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Extract from a report written for this exercise. 'Complaints about the new intake form cluster in the six weeks after each annual deadline. We checked whether this reflects where the deadline falls by comparing four years: in two years the deadline fell in a month with an open holiday fortnight and the cluster was absent, and in two years it fell outside one and the cluster was present each time. When the first of these patterns was found we had already begun looking for any period in which complaints rose, having suspected a link with the deadline in week three. The four years are the only years for which complaint logs were kept in the same form.'

questions.stem: What does the fifth sentence do to the strength of the second finding?

options.text: It shows the pattern was checked across four years, so finding it is stronger than a pattern seen in one year
options.misconception: credits the report with a virtue it has, while ignoring what the sentence says about how the search was done

options.text: It shows the suspicion was reasonable, so a pattern later found cannot fairly be called a coincidence
options.misconception: treats the reasonableness of a prior hunch as evidence for the pattern it turned up

options.text: It shows the holiday fortnight was not the real cause, so the deadline link is the one the evidence supports
options.misconception: draws a conclusion the report nowhere states about which of the two factors was acting

options.text: It shows the pattern was being sought, so finding it is less surprising than a pattern the analyst would have missed

questions.explanation: The report discloses something about its own method that most reports would leave out, and the disclosure matters. Someone who begins looking for periods in which complaints rose will find such periods; the four years were searched in a way that made a deadline cluster reasonably likely to appear, and a cluster that turns up after a targeted search carries less evidential weight than one that turned up unprompted across the whole record. The comparison across four years is the part of the design that answers this, and it is a real answer: two years with the fortnight show no cluster, two without do. What survives is a claim of moderate strength, and a group is entitled to prefer the version of the report that says so. The other three options read the sentence as adding support, when it is a disclosure about how the finding was reached.
questions.hint: Ask how the search was conducted, and what a targeted search would tend to turn up.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An account that would swallow any outcome
questions.learningObjective: explain why an explanation is weakened by the ease with which it can absorb contrary facts
questions.stem: Explain why an explanation is weakened by the ease with which it can be made to fit any outcome, and what a reader should look for instead.

answer.exemplar: An explanation is a claim about what should have been observed, so the test of it is whether the record could have come out otherwise. An account that can be adjusted until it fits whatever happened has not been tested at all: it has been made true by being flexible, and flexibility of that kind is a property of the account rather than a fact discovered about the case. A committee that hears 'the group is understaffed', and then hears that the low turnout happened in the week of a storm and also in the week of a timetable clash, has been given a claim that fits the whole term. What the reader should ask for instead is the shape of the claim: does it name a period, a population, and a direction, and does it say what would have been observed if it were false? A group may then bring forward the weeks it does not fit and ask for an account of those. If the explanation can be repaired to cover them, that is progress; if every repair empties it of content, the group has been offered a description of its own discomfort in the grammar of a cause. The practical test is cheap to state and worth applying: write down the two outcomes the account says could not both have happened, and check whether the group has seen them.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that an explanation is a claim about what should have been observed, so the test of it is whether the record could have come out otherwise; that an account adjusted until it fits is made true by its flexibility rather than by anything in the case; and that the repair is to ask the account to name a period, a population, a direction, and an outcome that would have falsified it. It should end with something runnable, such as writing down the two outcomes the account says could not both have happened and checking whether either was ever seen.
questions.hint: Ask what the account says would have happened if it were wrong, and whether anyone was ever in a position to notice.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Eliminating an account on scope rather than preference
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an account ruled out by the record from one merely not preferred
questions.stem: Two accounts of a fall in seminar attendance are offered. The record shows attendance dropped sharply only in the three weeks when a building fault closed one wing, and the rooms used in those weeks were larger. What has been established?

options.text: That the larger rooms are the cause, since they are the only change the record puts inside the period
options.misconception: picks the surviving candidate and promotes it, when the record excludes rather than establishes anything

options.text: That neither account can be tested, since both were formed after the fall was already known
options.misconception: objects to accounts formed after the fact, which is a general worry and not a finding about these two

options.text: That an account blaming the wing closure is inconsistent with when the fall occurred, which is a different kind of finding
That the wing closure is the cause, since the fall and the closure happened in the same three weeks
options.misconception: reports the effect of the check as its conclusion, having already ruled the closure out by timing

questions.explanation: An account that says the fall would have happened in the weeks the building was shut is ruled out by a record of when the fall actually happened, and being ruled out this way is a stronger position than being preferred. The room can state what the closure account would have predicted and check the prediction; it failed. That said, ruling one out says nothing about whether the remaining candidate is right, and the option that promotes it is the mistake students make most often here: a short list of survivors is not a finding. The remaining account would have to be tested in its own turn, and the honest statement of the group's position is that one candidate has been excluded and one has not been examined.
questions.hint: Ask what the excluded account predicted, and whether the record agrees with the prediction.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A source that does not yet exist in the record
questions.learningObjective: recognise an explanation whose supporting document postdates the period it explains

stimulus.kind: archive note written for this question
stimulus.body: Archive note written for this exercise. 'Box 14: unsigned, undated. One page in the same hand throughout, on the letterhead of the regional water office. It reports that residents of the Lower Wolds complained repeatedly of a taste in the mains, that the office logged eleven such complaints in March, and that the office informed the household it was logged. The office's own complaint ledger for March shows the eleven entries, and the ledger for April shows four more. The office did not begin recording taste complaints in a separate column until the following January, and the page in Box 14 is listed in the catalogue as a press handout, undated, from no later than the following spring.'

questions.stem: A writer uses Box 14 to show that the water office was formally recording taste complaints in March. On what ground does the use fail?

options.text: The page is unsigned, so nothing on it can be attributed to the office that wrote it
options.misconception: claims an attribution failure the note does not supply, since letterhead and the ledger entries both support it

options.text: The catalogue calls the page a handout, so its numbers must be treated as publicity rather than record
options.misconception: lets a catalogue genre label overturn the counts, which eleven ledger entries independently support

options.text: The page is undated, so it cannot be placed before the January change at all
options.misconception: reverses the dating the note supplies, which places the page no later than the following spring

options.text: The separate column began the following January, so a March complaint counted as a complaint of any kind and not as taste

questions.explanation: The writer's claim is about the office's recording practice, and the archive note is clear that the practice did not exist in March. The eleven complaints in the ledger are real and the page's summary of them is corroborated, so the box is good evidence that residents complained and that the office logged something; what it cannot show is that the office was classifying those complaints by taste, because the column that would hold that classification did not exist until the following January. This is the ordinary place where a document used as evidence outruns the practice it documents: the events happened, the record was made, and the record is silent on the point the writer needs. The other three options each reject the page for a reason the note either answers or does not raise.
questions.hint: Ask when the office's recording practice changed, and whether the page was made before or after it changed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A prediction confirmed after it was named
questions.learningObjective: assess the evidential value of a prediction that the analyst made about data already in hand

stimulus.kind: report extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Extract from a report written for this exercise. 'Having read the intake logs from the previous year, we expected that the accounts which gave a reason for closing a case would take longest to close, since a reason takes longer to write than a one-word code. The expectation was recorded in the shared notebook on a Thursday, and every account in the previous year's logs was read that afternoon. In the previous year, 68 of 204 accounts closed within two working days and 47 of them gave a reason. The same year read at the weekly level contains a shorter closing time for reason-giving accounts in 9 of the 12 weeks; in the remaining 3 weeks no reason-giving account was closed at all, so no comparison was possible. The four years are the only years for which intake logs were kept in the same form.'

questions.stem: What is the difficulty with the report's treatment of the weekly figures?

options.text: The weeks contradict one another, so no account of the variation is possible from the logs
options.misconception: reads disagreement between weeks as though no account could exist, rather than as a claim to explain

options.text: The prediction was made after the logs were read, so the weeks where it holds are ones already seen to hold
The prediction is about accounts and the weeks are about time, so the two are measuring different things
options.misconception: objects to a change of unit that the report makes explicit when it links accounts to weeks

options.text: The figure of 47 sits inside the 68, so the reason-giving accounts are a subset and cannot be compared
options.misconception: treats a stated relationship as a bar to comparison, which is the ordinary way a rate is built

questions.explanation: A prediction earns its keep when it is made about data the analyst has not seen, and this one was not. The expectation about reason-giving accounts was recorded in the shared notebook, but every account from the previous year had already been read that afternoon, so the expectation was formed with the figures in view. Reading a week-by-week breakdown afterwards and finding that it holds in 9 of 12 is therefore much weaker than it looks: an analyst who has the data in mind can notice this pattern easily, and a pattern noticed is much easier to find than one overlooked. The group is right to ask what would settle it, and the answer is a year whose logs were not read before the expectation was written down. Until then the report can say what it saw and not what it expected in advance.
questions.hint: Ask when the expectation was written down relative to reading the accounts it was about.

questions.topic: Eliminating an account by assuming away the evidence
questions.learningObjective: recognise an elimination whose force depends on an assumption about the record

stimulus.kind: methods extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Methods extract written for this exercise. 'To test whether the late notice causes absences, we compared the teams notified in advance with those notified late, taking notification to have been timely when a message went out at least two working days before the shift. Of 12 teams notified late, 9 had a member absent on the day; of 11 teams notified in advance, 3 did. Teams were not assigned to notification groups: eight of the late-notified teams had asked for a change of shift in the same fortnight, and the office assigned those requests to the late group because the request had not reached the scheduler in time. We have no record of how many members knew of the shift before the message.'

options.text: The rule that put shift-change requests into the late group is exactly what the timing measure was meant to stand in for
The two groups are of different sizes, so a count of 9 against 3 cannot be compared at all
options.misconception: objects to sizes of 12 and 11, which are close enough that the comparison stands regardless

options.text: No record was kept of what members knew, so the difference may be entirely in what they were told privately
options.misconception: finds a real gap but makes it the whole objection, when the assignment rule is what undermines the comparison

options.text: The measure of timeliness was fixed in advance, so the design cannot have been shaped by the result
options.misconception: reassures the reader about a problem the extract does not raise, and misses where the bias entered

questions.explanation: The comparison is between groups the extract says were not assigned at random, and the assignment that produced them is the assignment at issue. The 9 against 3 therefore cannot separate the notice from the change of shift, and no conclusion about the notice follows from it in either direction. The missing record of what members knew is a genuine second weakness and the second option's complaint about sizes is not a problem at all, since 12 and 11 are near enough to compare. The fix is to look at teams that requested no change.
questions.hint: Ask how teams came to be in the two groups, and whether that matches the variable being tested.

The second option compares the measures with each other rather than with the reader's use of one for the other, which is why it does not answer the question asked.

options.misconception: turns the group's inability to decide into a verdict against both, which nothing in the record supports

options.text: The two accounts are really one account expressed twice, so the group should report a single cause
options.misconception: collapses two accounts into one, which the record's inability to separate them does not warrant

options.text: The record cannot choose between them, both fit what we hold, and the reason names what would settle it

options.misconception: reports a preference as though the record had produced a winner, when it produced a tie

A preference stated as a conclusion pretends the record chose; the rejection of both converts indecision into a finding; and the collapse into one account asserts an identity between two things the group has just been unable to tell apart, which is the opposite of what it knows. The weak version of the same verdict would say only that the group could not choose, which is honest and gives the reader nothing to do.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do with the verdict, and whether the record actually chose.

Look for the point where the two accounts predict different records, since that is where the test has teeth
Gather what the record shows at that point, since the divergence is worth nothing until it is checked
Report which account was excluded, which survived, and which is still untested, since all three are results

First the record, because a test run against a record nobody holds settles nothing and a group that skips this step routinely finds itself comparing two accounts with the facts. Second, the accounts as testable claims, because an account stated as a mood or a summary cannot be checked against anything. Third, the point of divergence, which is the only place the comparison has any power. Fourth, the check itself, since a divergence nobody looked at is a hypothesis. Fifth, the report, and the reason the last step is three-part is that surviving a test is not the same as being supported, and an untested survivor is a result a reader is entitled to know about.

options.misconception: reads present silence as a verdict on an earlier period, which is a claim about today and not then

That the dispute it describes really occurred, since the memo is the only record of the argument available

options.misconception: reads flexibility as proof of availability, while a notice is not a duty roster

options.misconception: discards the document wholesale, when its bias is in what it is for rather than in its contents

The letter is two years old, so nothing in it can be used to argue about a present state of affairs
options.misconception: insists on recency, which would make every historical record unusable for reconstructing what once happened

options.text: The dataset is still being cleaned, so the letter cannot be evidence that the delay was legitimate
options.misconception: confuses what the letter was about with whether its account of the delay is credible

options.misconception: supposes receiving a letter settles its contents, which is a claim about delivery and not about truth

The test the reader should have applied is what the document is for and who could act on it, which would have shown that no one was confessing to anything.
questions.hint: Ask what the letter was written to do, and who was entitled to read it as an answer.

questions.topic: What the absence of a record can be asked to show
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the inferences a missing record supports from the ones it cannot

stimulus.kind: memo written for this question
stimulus.body: Memo written for this exercise, found in the file. 'Three of the four workshops we ran last year have evaluation forms in the file. The fourth has none, and I have no memory of it taking place, though the room booking is in the calendar for a Tuesday evening in February. The other three forms were typed up by the coordinator within a week. I am not able to say why the fourth has nothing, and the file does not record who ran it.'

questions.stem: What can the group take from the absence of the fourth set of forms?

options.text: That the coordinator did the other three and withheld the fourth, since the pattern of the first three is clear
options.misconception: infers an intention from a pattern of three, which is a hypothesis the file does not support

options.text: That the February booking was a mistake, since nothing in the record shows a workshop took place
options.misconception: proposes an alternative to the gap without evidence, when the booking is itself a positive trace

options.text: That evaluations were not gathered or not written up for that workshop, which the file does not say why
That the fourth workshop was badly run, since a run that produced no feedback was a run that failed
options.misconception: supplies a verdict from an absence, where a missing form may mean an unrun or unwritten record

questions.explanation: A missing record is evidence that a record is missing, and the honest reading stops there. The group knows that the fourth workshop has no evaluation forms and that it does not know why, which is enough to say that no feedback was gathered in the file for that evening and none was written up within the week the others were. It is not enough to say the evening went badly, since a form may be absent because the workshop did not run, because it ran without one, or because the person who would have typed it was away. The first option is the most tempting, because three typed forms and a fourth untyped one does form a pattern, and a pattern in three cases is the raw material of a hypothesis rather than a conclusion about a person. The room booking is a positive trace, and treating the gap as though it voided every other trace is the opposite of reading the record.
questions.hint: Ask what the file positively contains, and how many steps separate that from a verdict on the evening.

questions.topic: A category applied to a period before it existed
questions.learningObjective: identify the anachronism in a historical document used to support a contemporary claim

stimulus.kind: report extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Extract from a report written for this exercise. 'Between 1908 and 1911 the town council minutes record repeated discussion of two categories of member: those who paid the full subscription and those admitted at a reduced rate on the nomination of a full member. The report describes the second group as a form of assisted membership and reads the discussion of their voting rights as a debate about inclusion. A footnote records that the words assisted membership, inclusion, and access were not used in the minutes, and that the reduced rate applied to anyone nominated by two full members, with no income test recorded anywhere in the volume.'

questions.stem: A reader disputes the report's reading of the debate. On what ground?

options.text: The minutes' own terms are nomination and rate, and the modern terms import a test the volume never records
The debate concerned voting rights, and a debate about voting cannot be a debate about inclusion at all
options.misconception: severs two topics the volume puts in the same discussion, and rules out a reading it does not refute

options.text: The nomination requirement required two full members, and a two-signature rule cannot exclude anyone by itself
options.misconception: replaces the disputed reading with a different rule, leaving the imported vocabulary unexamined

options.text: The volume is a minute book, and minute books are written to record decisions rather than arguments
options.misconception: rejects the volume as a genre, where the report's own use of it may still be sound

questions.explanation: The report reads a modern distinction into a record that does not carry it. A reader who wants the report's account tested should therefore ask what the reduced rate was for, and can start with the council's own minutes for the years in question, which may name a purpose the modern vocabulary conceals. The other options each attack something other than the imported vocabulary: one severs topics the volume joined, one supplies a different rule, and one dismisses the source as a genre without asking whether the genre fits.
questions.hint: Ask what the volume's own words were, and what the report's words bring with them.

questions.topic: What a document of one kind can be used to show
questions.learningObjective: match a document's kind to the claims it can carry
questions.stem: A seminar holds three documents about a dispute in its own history: the minute of the meeting at which the dispute was settled, a private letter complaining about it, and a notice posted afterwards asking members to comply. Which use of each is sound?

options.text: The minute for what was really felt, the letter for what was settled, the notice for what went undecided
options.misconception: swaps the documents over, assigning decision to a complaint and feeling to a record of vote

options.text: The letter for the terms of the settlement, since only a participant could state them accurately
options.misconception: makes a private complaint authoritative on terms, which the minute that recorded them is better placed to give

options.text: The notice for what the members believed, since a posted request shows what the group held
options.misconception: reads a compliance notice as a statement of belief, which is a different kind of claim entirely

options.text: The minute for what was decided, the letter for what one member felt, the notice for what members were told

questions.explanation: Each document is a record of a different act, and the act limits the claim. A minute records that a decision was taken and what it was, so it is the right source for terms; it is a poor source for what anyone thought, since a vote produces the same minute whether the room was satisfied or seething. A letter is one member's complaint, excellent evidence of that member's view at one moment and no evidence at all of the dispute's substance. A notice asking for compliance shows what the group wanted members to do afterwards, which is not the same as what anyone believed, and the difference matters when a reader wants to know whether a rule was accepted. Reading each document for the act it records is the whole of the method here, and it is why the three can sit in one file without any of them speaking for the others.
questions.hint: For each document, ask what act produced it, and what that act is capable of recording.

questions.topic: The place and date a document claims for itself
questions.learningObjective: identify the details a writer's own description of a document does not settle

stimulus.kind: archive note written for this question
stimulus.body: Archive note written for this exercise. 'Item 61. A single sheet in a fair copy, headed Report of the Sub-committee, with the words Fourth Avenue in the header and the date 14 March in the body. The paper watermark belongs to a mill that supplied the regional office from 1930. The volume was renumbered in 1955 and the catalogue records the sheet as 1941 on the strength of the watermark alone. A second sheet, a covering note in the same hand, is filed behind it, undated, and reads: forwarded per the request of the 3rd, which the secretary of the day wrote in the upper margin of every forwarding slip.'

options.text: The mill supplied the office from 1930, so a 1941 date falls inside the period the watermark can support
The mill supplied from 1930, so a 1941 date is impossible and the sheet must be catalogued again
options.misconception: turns a consistent watermark into a contradiction, when the period given includes the dated year

options.text: The covering note explains how the sheet reached the volume, so the date in the body may be the real one
options.misconception: uses a note about transmission as if it were evidence about when the sheet was written

options.text: The sheet is a fair copy, so the date in the body is a copy of a date and carries no weight at all
options.misconception: annuls the date entirely, rather than transferring the question to what the copy was made from

What the note does show is how thin the support is: the date rests on a single incidental trace, a mill's supply range, and a fair copy whose body date may simply reproduce an earlier original. The covering note explains transmission, not composition, so it says the sheet was forwarded and not when it was written. A fair copy is still evidence of the document it copies, and the sensible response is to look for the original, to check whether any other sheet in the volume is headed the same way, and to record the catalogue's date as inferred rather than established. The second option reads the supply period as excluding the year, which it does not.
questions.hint: Check whether the year the catalogue gives falls inside the period the watermark can establish.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A copy standing in for the thing it copies
questions.learningObjective: identify the losses a transcription introduces and what only the original can restore

stimulus.kind: memo written for this question
stimulus.body: Memorandum written for this exercise, filed by the group secretary. 'The two paragraphs below are typed copies of what I read from the notebook at the meeting, and I have marked in square brackets anything I could not read. First: the committee agreed to defer the decision until the following meeting, and [illegible] the grounds for deferral. Second: a member objected that the consultation had not been completed, and the chair replied [illegible] before moving on. I typed these on the evening of the meeting and have since checked them against nothing else, because the notebook is kept by the office and I have not asked for it back.'

questions.stem: A reader treats the memorandum as a record of what was said. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: The brackets show the secretary was careful, and marking a gap is itself evidence the meeting said little
options.misconception: reads a marking practice as a finding about content, which the two gaps cannot establish

options.text: The notebook is kept by the office, so the memorandum should be set aside until the notebook is produced
options.misconception: prohibits use of the copy, where the defect is confined to what the two gaps leave unknown

options.text: Two passages are unreadable, and both are where the substance of the objection and the grounds would be
The memorandum was typed on the evening, and anything written later than that is outside what it can show
options.misconception: finds a limit that supports the record's accuracy, since an evening account is closer to the event than a later one

questions.explanation: The gaps fall in the two places where the interesting content would be, which is the ordinary way transcription fails. What the memorandum establishes is that a decision was deferred and that a member objected on the ground that the consultation was unfinished; it cannot show what the grounds for deferral were, or what the chair said in answer, and those are the two places a reader would go next. The honest use is to report the part that survives and to name the part that does not, then to ask the office for the notebook. Typing on the evening is a point in the record's favour rather than against it, marking a gap shows care rather than emptiness, and setting the memorandum aside altogether would lose what it does establish, which is a fair amount.
questions.hint: Look at where the gaps sit in the passage, and ask what a reader would most want to know there.

questions.topic: What a copy of a summary can be asked to support
questions.learningObjective: identify the document that must be produced before a quoted claim can be weighed
questions.stem: A seminar's file holds a photocopy of a paragraph in a printed report, which quotes a newspaper's account of a hearing and adds the sentence: the hearing also discussed funding. What is the file's position on that last sentence?

options.text: It is established, since the group holds a copy of the paragraph in which the sentence appears
options.misconception: confuses holding a copy of a claim with having evidence for the claim it makes

options.text: It is unreliable, since a photocopy cannot be trusted to reproduce a document accurately at all
options.misconception: dismisses a class of document wholesale, which would leave most archives unusable

options.text: It is secondhand twice over, so it may be used only where the original report is unavailable
options.misconception: sets a rule about how many removes a claim may have, which is not how weighing works

options.text: It is a claim in a document the group holds, and weighing it requires the report the copy came from

questions.explanation: The file establishes one thing and leaves another open. It establishes that a report the group does not hold makes the claim that the hearing discussed funding, which is worth having, since it tells the group where to look and gives the claim a traceable origin. It does not establish that the claim is true, and the number of removes between the group and the hearing is not what decides the matter; what decides it is whether the group can get to the document that asserts it and see what it rests on. So the sensible step is to write to the publisher for the paragraph and its source, and the sensible interim statement is that a report of unspecified standing makes the claim. Treating the copy as proof of the claim and treating it as worthless are the two errors at either end, and the first is the commoner one in seminars that are short of time.
questions.hint: Ask what the group holds, and which document the claim in it would have to be checked against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What survives, and what the surviving record is evidence of
questions.learningObjective: state why the contents of an archive reflect its keepers and not only its period
questions.stem: Explain why the contents of an archive reflect the people who kept it as well as the period it covers, and what a reader should do about it.

answer.exemplar: An archive is a set of decisions about what was worth keeping, and each decision was made by somebody with a purpose. A registry in the 1930s preserved applications for posts, disputes with suppliers, and minutes, because those were the papers an office needed in order to administer; it discarded circulars, telephone messages, and the working notes that preceded a decision, because nobody could imagine needing them. Two hundred years later the volume is a faithful record of the office's paperwork and a very poor record of the work. The reader who takes it as a sample of the period is reading the archivist's judgement as though it were the past's own, and the error has a direction: what is missing is missing for a reason connected to its own unimportance at the time of keeping, so gaps correlate with the ordinary and the routine, and the archive over-represents disputes, applications, and anything that had to be justified. The repair is to treat the contents as a claim about what mattered to the keeper. Ask what kind of paperwork this office was required to produce, which act of writing is over-represented, and what a matter would have had to look like to survive. Then read the survivors against the question: a volume of disputes tells a group that disputes were worth documenting here, which is a real fact about how the office was run, and not a count of how often they occurred.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that an archive is a set of keeping decisions and that each was made by somebody with a purpose; that the surviving set therefore over-represents whatever the keeper needed and what had to be justified, and under-represents the routine; that the missing is missing for a reason connected to its own apparent unimportance at the time; and that the reader is in danger of taking the keeper's judgement for the past's. It should end with the repair, which is to read the contents as a claim about what mattered to whoever kept them, and to use the kind of paperwork the office was required to produce as the explanation of the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of paper the office needed in order to do its work, and what that says about what was kept.
