questions.topic: Two reports that do not corroborate each other
questions.learningObjective: identify repetition of a single source as something other than confirmation
questions.stem: A paper reports a rise in complaints. A report on the same year also reports a rise, and cites that paper for the figure. A member claims the second confirms the first. What is the difficulty with the claim?

options.text: The second takes its figure from the first, so the agreement is one source appearing in two places
The two reports are not independent, so only one of them may ever be cited at all
options.misconception: makes citation depend on independence, where a repeated figure is worth citing as a repeated figure

options.text: The second adds nothing, since a report may only confirm a paper it has read closely
options.misconception: supplies a reading condition the claim never invoked, which is not what makes the pair non-corroborating

options.text: The claim is unavailable to members, since confirming a paper is itself a contribution to be credited
options.misconception: converts a rule about evidence into a rule about credit, which the argument does not raise

questions.explanation: Confirmation is a relation between chains of reporting, not a count of documents. When the second report's figure comes from the first, the two share every step that matters and the second adds no observation of its own; the figure has been seen twice by the same eye. The second report is still worth holding, since it tells the group that the figure circulated and how it was described at the time, but it cannot be cited as though it were a second sighting. What would raise the count is a body that reached the number by its own route, and a group asking that question should be specific about it: a separate return, a differently gathered series, a local count. The other options each convert a point about evidence into a rule about what may be cited or credited, which is not what the claim needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the second report did besides copy, and where its figure came from.

options.misconception: assumes a single convention, where the two counts may cover different parts of the meeting

options.text: That somebody came or went uncounted, which is the ordinary explanation for any difference in a roll call
options.misconception: names one possible cause as settled, when the group's own list suggests a difference of rule instead

That the group's own list settles it, and the count closest to 19 is the one the group should record
options.misconception: picks a winner by proximity, which chooses between conventions without identifying either

The group's list of 19 sitting between 18 and 20 is exactly what that looks like, since a list of names and a head count often differ by the late arrivals the count includes. The productive step is to ask each member what their figure counted, in writing, and then to fix the group's rule for the future. The first option assumes a single convention where there may be three, the second picks one cause as though it were established, and the fourth resolves the conflict by arithmetic without ever finding out what either number was a count of.
questions.hint: Ask each member what their number counted, before deciding which number is right.

questions.topic: Rates computed over case sets that grow
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rising rate across teams need not mean a rising disposition to reject

stimulus.body: Memorandum written for this exercise. The three teams see nested sets of complaints. The intake team saw 140 and upheld 9. The investigation team saw all 140 of those plus 70 more, so 210, and upheld 31. The hearing team saw all 210 plus 35 more, so 245, and upheld 52. The memo concludes: 'The share upheld rises at each stage, from 6 per cent at intake to 21 per cent at hearing, and the hearing team is therefore the most careful of the three.' The memo names the regional service statistics and the department's annual return as its sources, and both returns take the intake figures as their starting point.

questions.stem: What does the arithmetic in the memorandum show about the conclusion drawn from it?

options.text: All three teams use one threshold, so the rising shares measure the teams and not their case sets
options.misconception: asserts a common rule the memo nowhere states and which the nesting itself makes doubtful

options.text: Each team saw a larger case set, and a rising share is what a larger set of this kind produces
The shares rise at three successive stages, which is too regular a pattern to come from nothing
options.misconception: reads a monotone rise as significance, which nested denominators produce by construction

options.text: The hearing team saw the most complaints, and a team that sees more is a team that rejects more
options.misconception: confuses volume with rate, which are the two quantities the memo has kept apart by name

questions.explanation: The three shares are 9 of 140, which is 6.4 per cent, 31 of 210, which is 14.8 per cent, and 52 of 245, which is 21.2 per cent, and the denominators are nested: every complaint the intake team saw, the investigation team saw too, and so on. Once a set grows by adding cases, the added cases need not share the first set's mix, and a rise in the rate is the ordinary consequence. The memo's arithmetic is correct and its inference is not, which is a combination worth learning to see. The figure that would settle the question is the cross-tabulation, which nobody has produced: the share upheld among the 140 both later teams also saw. If that is near 6 per cent, the rise came from the added cases; if it is near 21 per cent, the hearing team is doing something the memo can then describe. The second-stage sources also descend from the intake figures, so they add no independent check.
questions.hint: Check whether the three teams' case sets contain one another, and what adding cases to a set does to its rate.

questions.topic: Apparent agreement resting on one origin
questions.learningObjective: assess how many observations a set of concurring reports actually contains
questions.stem: Three bodies' reports on a new local service all give the same satisfaction figure, and each of the three cites a fourth body for it. A member says three bodies agreeing is corroboration. What does the arrangement show?

options.text: That the three bodies checked the figure independently, and so the agreement is a real one
options.misconception: treats citation as a check, which is what the group has specifically been told did not happen

options.text: That the fourth body is the more reliable, and its figure may be preferred on that ground
options.misconception: confuses being the origin of a figure with being right about it, which are separate questions

options.text: That a figure that travels this way is false, since genuine figures do not spread so easily
options.misconception: concludes the figure is wrong from its circulation, which is a different and unfounded claim

options.text: That the fourth body produced the figure, so one figure is in three places rather than three findings

questions.explanation: The arrangement is a broadcast, not a count. Three bodies each naming the fourth as their source means three reports and one observation, and the agreement a member is pointing at is an artefact of the fourth body's figure being repeated rather than checked. This is the commonest way apparent consensus arises in documentary work, and it is invisible unless someone traces the citations, which is why the exercise of tracing them is worth the time it takes. The figure is not thereby false, and the fourth body is not thereby right; the two questions the group should ask are where the fourth body got the number and whether anybody gathered it independently. The other options each convert the observation into a verdict, in one direction or the other, when what the arrangement establishes is a fact about the reporting.
questions.hint: Ask where each of the three figures came from, and count the places the number was gathered.

That 33 is the attendance, since the standing orders ask for the count at the close and only one sheet has it

options.misconception: assumes the second sheet is a faithful count, which is the assumption the arithmetic is testing

options.misconception: presumes both returns counted the same events, which is exactly what the footnote disputes

That the exchange's figure is the one to use, since a different body is by definition a better count

options.misconception: counts a document that names two upstream sources as though naming made a new observation

options.text: One, because every document in the set descends from A and none observes the figure for itself

options.misconception: converts proximity to a decision into knowledge of what produced it, which are separate things

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A document whose wording supports two incompatible readings
questions.learningObjective: identify the evidence that would separate two strong readings of the same text

stimulus.kind: bureau memorandum written for this question
stimulus.body: Memorandum written for this exercise, headed Bureau of Settlement, and dated in its heading only by the quarter. 'District offices will report persons seeking employment in the district. No one is to be placed in the district without a certificate from this office. The certificate fee is one shilling, refundable on departure. Persons refusing the certificate are to be reported to the district clerk by name and by former occupation.' The archive note records that the volume contains two other memoranda for the same quarter, one directing that no one is to be assigned work in the district without a certificate, and one listing occupations that were not to be entered without a certificate; and that the certificates for that quarter are filed under a heading using the word admission, while the returns of persons are filed under a heading using the word claims.

questions.stem: A reader concludes from the memo that the bureau would place people in the district. What is the strongest supported judgement?

options.text: That the memo settles the question, so the parallel memoranda and the filing headings are beside the point
options.misconception: asserts the text is decisive, where the archive note shows the same office used both formulas

options.text: That the bureau would place people, since the certificate is a condition of a placement that would otherwise happen
That the bureau would place nobody, since a clause beginning no one is to be placed forbids the act outright
options.misconception: reads the clause as absolute and ignores the certificate that the same clause makes a condition

options.text: That the two clauses are silent on who would place them, so the reading rests on the parallel memoranda
options.misconception: misses that the certificate presupposes a placement, which is a real fact in the text

questions.explanation: The strongest reading of the memo is that it describes a screening rule rather than a prohibition, and it has a real feature to point to: a certificate cannot be a condition of an act nobody performs, and a refundable fee on departure only makes sense if departures are expected. The strongest reading the other way is that people seeking employment and a district in which no one is to be placed are simply incompatible, and a bureau with no work to offer was not placing anybody. What separates the two is in the archive note rather than in the memo. The office used the same formula for work and for settlement in the same quarter, so placement meant assignment in one document and admission in another; and the certificates are filed under admission while the claims are filed under claims, which suggests a person was admitted somewhere and that the certificate recorded it. A careful reader would say the reading is probable, say what would settle it, and not treat a memorandum as self-explaining.
questions.hint: Ask why a certificate would be needed, refundable, and filed under a heading of its own.

options.misconception: claims the letter settles the request, which the writer explicitly declines to do

questions.hint: Ask what in the letter is a fact about the case and what is a fact about the conversation.

The officer also wrote in the same term that two of the three late sessions had run long, and the final count of late sessions rose from 4 to 11. options.misconception: mistakes a rival explanation for a broken link, which the chain does not need to survive

options.text: At the step from the officer's note to the count of late sessions, since the note gives no count at all

options.misconception: objects to the use of a percentage to report a rise, which is what percentages are for

options.text: At the step from the tablets to faster signing, since nobody recorded how long signing took before or after

questions.explanation: An account is worth pursuing when it says something the accounts already held do not, and the extension-request pattern does: a new deadline and a heavier marking load both say nothing about requests. The prediction also lands in a record the group has not looked at, the request log, which is what makes pursuing it cheap and the outcome informative. Counting the requests is the check, and it is worth doing, but the count is not the test: a large number of requests would be consistent with a spike caused by the new deadline and with a spike caused by the load, and the discriminating question is whether requests cluster in the fortnight before each deadline rather than throughout the term. The other options substitute availability, standing, and the check itself for the test, and each of them is a practical question the group should also be asking.
questions.hint: Ask what the third account says should be in the record that the two existing accounts do not predict.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The premise a group is unwilling to state in public
questions.learningObjective: assess what a group's refusal to name its own standard is evidence of
questions.stem: A group has argued for three weeks that its shared log is working, and every member privately says the entries are thin. A member proposes stating the group's own standard of a sufficient entry, and the group declines, saying the proposal invites criticism. Four readings of the refusal follow. Which is the strongest supported judgement?

options.text: The group is applying a standard it will not name, which is why naming it feels dangerous to them
options.misconception: assumes the group has a settled unnamed standard, which the case does not establish either way

options.text: The group is protecting a log the members have agreed is working and must not be doubted
options.misconception: takes a public agreement at face value as a settled finding about the log's quality

options.text: The group is avoiding a question it has raised, and a group that does so has not settled it
The group has misunderstood a proposal that asks for a standard rather than an admission of failure
options.misconception: supposes a misreading, where the refusal and the reason given fit together well enough

questions.explanation: The group has identified the question, since the members' private doubts and the public claim are both present and neither settles the matter, and it has then declined the step that would settle it. That is what avoidance of this kind looks like, and the judgement is supported whatever the members' reasons happen to be. The reasons themselves are not silly. Naming a standard creates a test the group may fail, a member who is unsure of one of their own entries has a real interest in not being shown the yardstick, and a group three weeks into an argument about a log may want to finish the argument before auditing itself. The first two readings are stronger as accounts of the members' motives than the case supports, since nothing shows either a settled unnamed standard or a settled belief that the log works. The fourth is available, but it needs a mistake nobody has described. A group can test this cheaply without publishing anything: draft a standard privately and see how many entries meet it.
questions.hint: Ask what a group avoids, and whether the avoidance fits any of the reasons given for it.
